docs.title: 1. Data
docs.text:
This report generates and measures synthetic point clouds (Exercises 1 and 2) and prepares a real Kaggle dataset for a tanh network (Exercise 3). The thread is the spread of the data: how far a cloud extends, in which direction, and what that does to the boundaries a network would need. Statement: Exercises → 1. Data (2026.2).

How to re-run. From the repository root:

python docs/exercises/data/code/main.py

The script regenerates every figure in figures/ and prints every number quoted below, one labelled line per number. Exercise 3 needs Kaggle's train.csv (see Getting the data); without it the script still runs Exercises 1 and 2 and prints the download instructions.

Seed policy. main.py creates the report's only generator, rng = np.random.default_rng(42), and passes it to ex1(rng), ex2(rng) and ex3(rng) in statement order. No module creates a generator of its own, so the whole report is one reproducible random stream: running the script twice gives byte-identical figures and identical numbers. No model is trained anywhere; scikit-learn is used only for PCA (Exercise 2) and for preprocessing (Exercise 3).

main.py
"""Single entry point of the "1. Data" report.

Run from the repository root:

    python docs/exercises/data/code/main.py

It creates the report's ONE random generator, rng = np.random.default_rng(42),
and passes it to the three exercises in statement order (1 -> 2 -> 3). The
exercise modules never create a generator of their own, so every figure in
../figures/ and every number printed below is identical on every run.

Exercise 3 needs Kaggle's Spaceship Titanic train.csv in code/raw/. When the
file is missing, Exercises 1 and 2 still run and the script prints how to get it.

    ex2(rng, FIG_DIR)                     # Figures 4-5

    else:

        print("=" * 70)
        print(f"Expected file: {CSV_PATH}")
        print("To get it (requires a Kaggle account):")
        print(f"  1. Open {KAGGLE_URL}")
        print("  2. Sign in, open the 'Data' tab and accept the competition rules.")
        print("  3. Download train.csv (or the zip and extract train.csv from it).")
        print(f"  4. Save it as {CSV_PATH.relative_to(CODE_DIR.parents[3]).as_posix()}")
        print("     (the folder code/raw/ is git-ignored), then run this script again.")
        print("  CLI alternative (needs a Kaggle API token): "
              "kaggle competitions download -c spaceship-titanic")
        print("     downloads spaceship-titanic.zip; extract train.csv from it.")

docs.title: Exercise 1
docs.text:
Point clouds: geometry and spread in 2D. The only random draw in this exercise is one array of standard-normal noise \(z\) of shape \((4, 100, 2)\) from the report's rng, turned into points by \(x = \mu_k + s\,\sigma_k \odot z\) (independent per-axis Gaussians). Item A uses \(s = 1\); item B reuses the same noise for every \(s \in \{0.5, 1, 2, 4\}\), so the four datasets differ only in spread and the \(s = 1\) dataset of item B is exactly the dataset of Figure 1. Separation ratios use the specified parameters, the mixing rate is plain NumPy geometry against the four true means, and an exact convex-hull test decides whether a pair of classes can be split by one straight line.

Driver of Exercise 1 (ex1): runs A → B → C and prints every number ex1_point_clouds.py
def ex1(rng, fig_dir):
    """Run items A, B and C in statement order and print every quoted number."""
    print("=" * 70)
    print("EXERCISE 1 - Point clouds")
    print("=" * 70)

    # ---- A: generate the clouds (the only random draw of Exercise 1) --------
    noise = draw_noise(rng)
    X, y = make_clouds(noise, scale=1.0)
    print(f"[1A] samples: {len(X)} total, per class: {np.bincount(y).tolist()}")
    for k in range(N_CLASSES):
        m, sd = X[y == k].mean(axis=0), X[y == k].std(axis=0, ddof=1)
        print(f"[1A] class {k}: sample mean = ({m[0]:.2f}, {m[1]:.2f}), "
              f"sample std = ({sd[0]:.2f}, {sd[1]:.2f})  "
              f"[specified mu = {MEANS[k].tolist()}, sigma = {STDS[k].tolist()}]")
    plot_figure1(X, y, fig_dir / "fig1.png")

    # ---- B: the same classes at four spreads ---------------------------------
    # The SAME noise is reused for every s, so the four datasets differ only in
    # spread: point i of class k sits at mu_k + s * sigma_k * z_i for all s.
    datasets = {s: make_clouds(noise, scale=s) for s in SCALES}
    xlim, ylim = plot_figure2(datasets, fig_dir / "fig2.png")
    print(f"[1B] Figure 2 shared limits: x in [{xlim[0]:.2f}, {xlim[1]:.2f}], "
          f"y in [{ylim[0]:.2f}, {ylim[1]:.2f}]")

    rows = separation_ratios(scale=1.0)
    print(f"[1B] sigma_bar_k = (sigma_x + sigma_y) / 2 at s = 1: "
          f"{dict(enumerate(STDS.mean(axis=1).round(4).tolist()))}")
    print("[1B] separation ratio at s = 1 (specified parameters):")
    for i, j, dist, denom, r in rows:
        print(f"[1B]   pair ({i},{j}): ||mu_i-mu_j|| = {dist:.4f}, "
              f"sigma_bar_i+sigma_bar_j = {denom:.4f}, r = {r:.4f}")
    i, j, *_, r_min = min(rows, key=lambda row: row[-1])
    print(f"[1B] smallest r_ij at s = 1: pair ({i},{j}) r = {r_min:.4f}")
    for s in SCALES:
        print(f"[1B] smallest r_ij at s = {s:g}: r_{i}{j} = r/s = {r_min / s:.4f}")
    print(f"[1B] r_{i}{j}(s) = 1 when s = {r_min:.4f}")
    for a, b, *_ in rows:
        print(f"[1B]   directional ratio (spread along mu_i -> mu_j) pair ({a},{b}) "
              f"at s = 1: {directional_ratio(a, b):.4f}")

    rates = {s: mixing_rate(*datasets[s]) for s in SCALES}
    for s in SCALES:
        n_mixed = int(round(rates[s] * len(X)))
        print(f"[1B] mixing rate at s = {s:g}: {rates[s]:.4f} "
              f"({100 * rates[s]:.2f}%, {n_mixed} of {len(X)} points)")
    for s in SCALES:
        M = mixing_matrix(*datasets[s])
        mixed = {f"{a}->{b}": int(M[a, b]) for a in range(N_CLASSES)
                 for b in range(N_CLASSES) if a != b and M[a, b] > 0}
        print(f"[1B] s = {s:g} mixed points by (true -> nearest center): {mixed}")
    # Exact pairwise check: if every pair is linearly separable, a set of straight
    # lines (one per pair, one-vs-one voting) classifies all 400 points correctly.
    bad_pairs = {s: non_separable_pairs(*datasets[s]) for s in SCALES}
    for s in SCALES:
        print(f"[1B] s = {s:g} pairs NOT linearly separable: "
              f"{bad_pairs[s] if bad_pairs[s] else 'none'}")
    first_bad_s = min(s for s in SCALES if bad_pairs[s])
    print(f"[1B] first scale with a pair that no straight line separates: s = {first_bad_s:g} "
          f"(smallest r there: r_{i}{j} = {r_min / first_bad_s:.4f})")
    plot_figure3(rates, (i, j), r_min, first_bad_s, fig_dir / "fig3.png")

    # ---- C: sketch on Figure 1 ------------------------------------------------
    n_wrong = plot_sketch(X, y, fig_dir / "fig1_sketch.png")
    edges = sorted(voronoi_edges((X[:, 0].min() - 1, X[:, 0].max() + 1),
                                 (X[:, 1].min() - 1, X[:, 1].max() + 1)))
    print(f"[1C] sketched boundary segments between classes: {edges}")
    print(f"[1C] points on the wrong side of the sketch at s = 1: {n_wrong}")
    return rates, rows

# Parameters copied from the statement: one row per class, columns (x, y).
MEANS = np.array([[2.0, 3.0],    # class 0
                  [5.0, 6.0],    # class 1
                  [8.0, 1.0],    # class 2
                  [15.0, 4.0]])  # class 3
STDS = np.array([[0.8, 2.5],
                 [1.2, 1.9],
                 [0.9, 0.9],
                 [0.5, 2.0]])
N_PER_CLASS = 100                 # 4 classes x 100 = 400 samples
N_CLASSES = len(MEANS)
SCALES = (0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0)     # spread multipliers of item B

def draw_noise(rng):
    """Draw the standard-normal noise z ~ N(0, 1) for every class, point and axis.

    Shape (4, 100, 2). Each axis gets its own independent draw, so the clouds
    are independent per-axis Gaussians (diagonal covariance), as specified.
    """
    return rng.standard_normal((N_CLASSES, N_PER_CLASS, 2))


def make_clouds(noise, scale=1.0):
    """Turn the noise into labelled points: x = mu_k + (s * sigma_k) * z.

    Broadcasting applies class k's mean and (scaled) standard deviation to all
    100 points of that class. Returns X with shape (400, 2) and integer labels y.
    """
    points = MEANS[:, None, :] + scale * STDS[:, None, :] * noise
    X = points.reshape(-1, 2)                                  # stack the 4 classes
    y = np.repeat(np.arange(N_CLASSES), N_PER_CLASS)           # 0...0, 1...1, ...
    return X, y

docs.title: B — More or less spread out
docs.text:
How the four datasets are drawn. The noise \(z\) from item A is drawn once and rescaled: point \(i\) of class \(k\) sits at \(\mu_k + s\,\sigma_k \odot z_i\) for every \(s\). The means never move, all standard deviations are multiplied by \(s\), and because the noise is shared, any change between the datasets is caused by the spread alone, not by a new random draw. This gives 4 datasets of 4 classes (100 points per class each).

1. Figure 2. The four subplots share the same axis limits, \(x_1 \in [-7.38, 21.06]\) and \(x_2 \in [-18.95, 34.57]\): the bounding box of all four datasets plus a 5% margin. At \(s = 0.5\) the clouds are compact islands; at \(s = 4\) they cover the whole window.

ex1_point_clouds.py
def plot_figure2(datasets, path):
    """Figure 2: one subplot per scale s, all sharing the SAME axis limits."""
    # Shared limits = bounding box of all four datasets plus a 5% margin, so the
    # widest cloud (s = 4) fits and the four panels are directly comparable.
    all_pts = np.vstack([X for X, _ in datasets.values()])
    lo, hi = all_pts.min(axis=0), all_pts.max(axis=0)
    pad = 0.05 * (hi - lo)
    xlim, ylim = (lo[0] - pad[0], hi[0] + pad[0]), (lo[1] - pad[1], hi[1] + pad[1])

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(11, 9), sharex=True, sharey=True)
    for ax, (s, (X, y)) in zip(axes.ravel(), datasets.items()):
        _scatter_classes(ax, X, y, size=9, alpha=0.6)
        _mark_centers(ax, size=110, label=False)
        ax.set_xlim(xlim)
        ax.set_ylim(ylim)
        ax.set_title(f"s = {s:g}  (all $\\sigma$ multiplied by {s:g})")
        ax.set_xlabel("$x_1$")
        ax.set_ylabel("$x_2$")
        ax.tick_params(labelbottom=True, labelleft=True)
        ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
    axes[0, 0].legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=8)
    fig.suptitle("Figure 2 - The same four classes at four spreads (identical axis limits)")
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(path, dpi=150)
    plt.close(fig)
    return xlim, ylim

Figure 2 — The same four classes at \(s = 0.5, 1, 2, 4\) with identical axis limits; the stars are the (unchanged) means.

2. Separation ratio at \(s = 1\). With \(\bar\sigma_k = (\sigma_{k,x} + \sigma_{k,y})/2\) computed from the specified parameters (\(\bar\sigma_0 = 1.65\), \(\bar\sigma_1 = 1.55\), \(\bar\sigma_2 = 0.90\), \(\bar\sigma_3 = 1.25\)):

\[ r_{ij} = \frac{\lVert \mu_i - \mu_j \rVert}{\bar\sigma_i + \bar\sigma_j} \] Pair \((i, j)\) \(\lVert \mu_i - \mu_j \rVert\) \(\bar\sigma_i + \bar\sigma_j\) \(r_{ij}\) at \(s = 1\) (0, 1) 4.2426 3.20 1.3258 (smallest) (0, 2) 6.3246 2.55 2.4802 (0, 3) 13.0384 2.90 4.4960 (1, 2) 5.8310 2.45 2.3800 (1, 3) 10.1980 2.80 3.6422 (2, 3) 7.6158 2.15 3.5422

The smallest ratio is \(r_{01} = 1.326\), between classes 0 and 1: their centers are only 1.33 "average spreads" apart. Every \(\bar\sigma_k\) is multiplied by \(s\) while the means stay put, so \(r_{ij}(s) = r_{ij}(1)/s\). At \(s = 2\), without generating anything, \(r_{01} = 1.3258 / 2 = 0.663\).

ex1_point_clouds.py
def separation_ratios(scale=1.0):
    """r_ij = ||mu_i - mu_j|| / (sigma_bar_i + sigma_bar_j) for the 6 pairs.

    Uses the SPECIFIED parameters (not sample estimates). sigma_bar_k is the
    average of the two axis standard deviations of class k, times the scale s,
    so r_ij(s) = r_ij(1) / s.
    """
    sigma_bar = scale * STDS.mean(axis=1)              # (sigma_x + sigma_y) / 2
    rows = []
    for i, j in combinations(range(N_CLASSES), 2):     # (0,1), (0,2), ..., (2,3)
        dist = np.linalg.norm(MEANS[i] - MEANS[j])
        rows.append((i, j, dist, sigma_bar[i] + sigma_bar[j],
                     dist / (sigma_bar[i] + sigma_bar[j])))
    return rows


def directional_ratio(i, j, scale=1.0):
    """Variant of r_ij that uses the spread ALONG the line joining the two centers.

    For a class with per-axis stds (sx, sy), the std of its projection onto the
    unit vector d = (dx, dy) is sqrt(dx^2 sx^2 + dy^2 sy^2). r_ij averages the
    two axes instead, so it ignores the direction in which each cloud is spread.
    """
    d = (MEANS[j] - MEANS[i]) / np.linalg.norm(MEANS[j] - MEANS[i])
    spread = lambda k: scale * np.sqrt(np.sum(d ** 2 * STDS[k] ** 2))  # noqa: E731
    return np.linalg.norm(MEANS[j] - MEANS[i]) / (spread(i) + spread(j))

3. Mixing rate. For each point we find the nearest of the four true means and count the points whose nearest mean is not their own class's:

\[ \text{mixing}(s) = \frac{1}{400} \sum_{n=1}^{400} \mathbb{1}\!\left[\arg\min_k \lVert x_n - \mu_k \rVert \neq y_n\right] \] \(s\) Mixing rate Mixed points Where they go (true class → nearest center) 0.5 0.25% 1 of 400 0→1: 1 1.0 5.00% 20 of 400 0→1: 8, 1→0: 6, 1→2: 6 2.0 20.25% 81 of 400 0↔1: 48, 1↔2: 18, 0↔2: 7, 2↔3: 7, 1→3: 1 4.0 43.00% 172 of 400 every pair except 0↔3; 0↔1: 57, 1↔2: 36, 0↔2: 34, 2↔3: 33, 1↔3: 12 ex1_point_clouds.py
def nearest_center(X):
    """Index of the closest TRUE class mean for every point (Euclidean)."""
    # (n, 1, 2) - (1, 4, 2) -> (n, 4, 2) differences -> (n, 4) distances.
    dists = np.linalg.norm(X[:, None, :] - MEANS[None, :, :], axis=2)
    return dists.argmin(axis=1)


def mixing_rate(X, y):
    """Fraction of points whose nearest center is NOT the mean of their class."""
    return float(np.mean(nearest_center(X) != y))


def mixing_matrix(X, y):
    """Counts M[true class, nearest-center class]; off-diagonal = mixed points."""
    M = np.zeros((N_CLASSES, N_CLASSES), dtype=int)
    np.add.at(M, (y, nearest_center(X)), 1)
    return M

4. Figure 3 and the separability threshold. The mixing rate counts errors of one particular set of straight lines: the nearest-center boundaries. To answer "from which \(s\) on can the clouds no longer be separated by straight lines?" exactly, the code also tests every pair of classes: two finite point sets can be split by a single straight line if and only if their convex hulls do not intersect. The test is pure geometry on the sampled points; nothing is fitted. If every pair is separable, a set of straight lines (one per pair, with one-vs-one voting) classifies all 400 points correctly.

\(s\) Pairs that no straight line separates Smallest ratio \(r_{01}\) 0.5 none 2.65 1.0 (0, 1), (1, 2) 1.33 2.0 (0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 2) 0.66 4.0 (0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3) 0.33

From \(s = 1\) on, the clouds can no longer be separated by straight lines. At \(s = 0.5\) the nearest-center lines still misplace one point (0.25%), but the hull test shows a slightly moved line would fix it: all 6 pairs are linearly separable. At \(s = 1\) the convex hulls of classes 0 and 1 (and of 1 and 2) intersect, so any straight boundary between them misclassifies at least one point, and the mixing rate is 5.00%. At that point the smallest ratio is \(r_{01} = 1.33\) (it was 2.65 at \(s = 0.5\)). The distance between the centers of classes 0 and 1 (4.24) is then only 1.33 times the sum of their average spreads (3.20), so the two clouds meet roughly 1.3 average spreads from each center, and with 100 points per class a handful of points of each class reach past that meeting zone: the 14 points 0↔1 of the mixing table. \(r_{01}\) crosses 1 at \(s = 1.33\); at \(s = 2\) it is 0.66, the distance between the centers is smaller than the sum of the spreads, and the mixing rate jumps to 20.25%.

Gaussian tails never end, so in theory any two of these clouds overlap at every \(s\), and a large enough sample is never linearly separable. The threshold \(s = 1\) describes these 100-point samples. With more points per class the extreme tails would reach further and separability would be lost at a smaller \(s\).

\(r_{ij}\) is a summary, not an exact criterion, because it averages the two axis spreads and ignores their direction. Pair (1, 2) already fails at \(s = 1\) although \(r_{12} = 2.38\), while pair (0, 2), with almost the same \(r_{02} = 2.48\), is still separable at \(s = 1\) and fails only at \(s = 2\). Measuring each cloud's spread along the line joining the two centers (unit vector \(d\)), \(\sigma_{k,\text{dir}} = \sqrt{d_x^2\sigma_{k,x}^2 + d_y^2\sigma_{k,y}^2}\), explains the difference. That ratio is 2.21 for (1, 2), because class 1 is widest along \(y\), the direction of \(\mu_2 - \mu_1\). It is 3.17 for (0, 2), because class 0's large \(\sigma_y = 2.5\) is almost perpendicular to \(\mu_2 - \mu_0\). For (0, 1) it is 1.23.

def convex_hull(P):
    """Vertices of the convex hull of 2-D points (Andrew's monotone chain)."""
    P = np.unique(P, axis=0)                 # sorted by x, then y

    def cross(o, a, b):                      # > 0 when o -> a -> b turns left
        return (a[0] - o[0]) * (b[1] - o[1]) - (a[1] - o[1]) * (b[0] - o[0])

    lower, upper = [], []
    for p in P:                              # lower chain, left to right
        while len(lower) >= 2 and cross(lower[-2], lower[-1], p) <= 0:
            lower.pop()
        lower.append(p)
    for p in P[::-1]:                        # upper chain, right to left
        while len(upper) >= 2 and cross(upper[-2], upper[-1], p) <= 0:
            upper.pop()
        upper.append(p)
    return np.array(lower[:-1] + upper[:-1])


def linearly_separable(A, B):
    """Exact test: can ONE straight line put all of A on one side and all of B on the other?

    Two finite point sets are linearly separable iff their convex hulls do not
    intersect, and two convex polygons are disjoint iff the normal of one of
    their edges is a separating axis (separating-axis theorem). So we project
    both sets onto every edge normal of both hulls and look for a gap.
    Pure geometry on the sampled points: nothing is fitted or trained.
    """
    for H in (convex_hull(A), convex_hull(B)):
        edges = np.roll(H, -1, axis=0) - H           # edge vectors of the hull
        normals = np.c_[-edges[:, 1], edges[:, 0]]   # one normal per edge
        pa, pb = A @ normals.T, B @ normals.T        # projections, (n, n_edges)
        gap = (pa.max(axis=0) < pb.min(axis=0)) | (pb.max(axis=0) < pa.min(axis=0))
        if gap.any():
            return True
    return False


def non_separable_pairs(X, y):
    """Class pairs (i, j) that no single straight line can separate."""
    return [(i, j) for i, j in combinations(range(N_CLASSES), 2)
            if not linearly_separable(X[y == i], X[y == j])]

docs.title: C — Analysis
docs.text:
1. Overlap at \(s = 1\); one or several linear boundaries? Figure 1 shows three situations. Class 3 is isolated: no point of any class is assigned to it or leaves it (all its ratios are \(\geq 3.54\)). Classes 1 and 2 only touch: 6 class-1 points are nearer to \(\mu_2\). Classes 0 and 1 interpenetrate: the tall class-0 cloud (\(\sigma_y = 2.5\)) reaches into class 1, with 8 + 6 = 14 points on the wrong side of their bisector. In total 20 of 400 points (5.00%) are closer to another center.

  • A single linear boundary cannot separate the four classes: one line divides the plane into only two half-planes, so at least two classes always share a side.
  • A set of linear boundaries does most of the job. The five bisector segments of the sketch below classify 380 of 400 points (95%), and class 3 alone needs just one line through the empty band visible in Figure 1. They cannot reach 100%: pairs (0, 1) and (1, 2) are not linearly separable (hull test), so no arrangement of straight lines with one convex region per class avoids errors there. Only a wiggly, non-convex boundary could, and that would be fitting the noise.

2. Sketch on Figure 1. The boundaries I expect a trained network to learn are the perpendicular bisectors between neighbouring centers. They are drawn as black segments over a copy of Figure 1, with each region tinted by its class. The segments are 0|1, 0|2, 1|2, 1|3 and 2|3 (classes 0 and 3 never meet). Concretely:

  • two steep segments (1|3 and 2|3) run through the empty band between the class-2 and class-3 clouds and isolate class 3;
  • the diagonal line \(x_1 + x_2 = 8\) (the bisector of \(\mu_0 = (2,3)\) and \(\mu_1 = (5,6)\)) cuts through the 0/1 overlap;
  • two shorter segments (0|2 and 1|2) meet at the point equidistant from \(\mu_0\), \(\mu_1\) and \(\mu_2\) and close off class 2 from classes 0 and 1.

A network with a few hidden units would produce a smoothed, slightly bent version of these segments, because unequal spreads shift the best boundary toward the narrower cloud. Where the clouds overlap it cannot do much better than the sketch: the circled points (20, all in the 0|1 and 1|2 overlap zones) sit on the wrong side.

ex1_point_clouds.py
def voronoi_edges(xlim, ylim, n=4000):
    """Pieces of the perpendicular bisectors that separate neighbouring means.

    For each pair (i, j) the bisector is the set of points equidistant to mu_i
    and mu_j. We sample that line densely inside the plot window and keep only
    the samples that are at least as close to mu_i (= mu_j) as to every other
    mean: those samples form the boundary segment between the two regions.
    Pairs whose bisector never survives (non-neighbours) are skipped.
    """
    edges = {}
    for i, j in combinations(range(N_CLASSES), 2):
        mid = (MEANS[i] + MEANS[j]) / 2
        d = MEANS[j] - MEANS[i]
        direction = np.array([-d[1], d[0]]) / np.linalg.norm(d)   # along the bisector
        t = np.linspace(-60, 60, n)
        pts = mid + t[:, None] * direction
        inside = ((pts[:, 0] >= xlim[0]) & (pts[:, 0] <= xlim[1]) &
                  (pts[:, 1] >= ylim[0]) & (pts[:, 1] <= ylim[1]))
        dists = np.linalg.norm(pts[:, None, :] - MEANS[None], axis=2)
        keep = inside & (dists[:, i] <= dists.min(axis=1) + 1e-9)
        if keep.any():
            edges[(i, j)] = pts[keep]
    return edges


def plot_sketch(X, y, path):
    """Copy of Figure 1 with the sketched (piecewise-linear) decision boundaries."""
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10.5, 6))
    xlim = (X[:, 0].min() - 1, X[:, 0].max() + 1)
    ylim = (X[:, 1].min() - 1, X[:, 1].max() + 1)

    # Light background tint: each grid cell takes the color of its nearest mean.
    gx, gy = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(*xlim, 400), np.linspace(*ylim, 400))
    region = nearest_center(np.c_[gx.ravel(), gy.ravel()]).reshape(gx.shape)
    ax.contourf(gx, gy, region, levels=np.arange(-0.5, N_CLASSES), alpha=0.12,
                cmap=ListedColormap(COLORS))

    _scatter_classes(ax, X, y)
    _mark_centers(ax)

    # The sketched boundaries: bisector segments between neighbouring means.
    for n_edge, ((i, j), seg) in enumerate(voronoi_edges(xlim, ylim).items()):
        ax.plot(seg[:, 0], seg[:, 1], color="black", linewidth=2,
                label="Sketched boundaries" if n_edge == 0 else None)

    # Points that fall on the wrong side of the sketch: the unavoidable errors.
    wrong = nearest_center(X) != y
    ax.scatter(*X[wrong].T, s=70, facecolors="none", edgecolors="black",
               linewidths=1.2, label=f"Wrong side of the sketch ({wrong.sum()} points)")

    ax.set_xlim(xlim)
    ax.set_ylim(ylim)
    ax.set_title("Figure 1 with sketched decision boundaries (s = 1)")
    ax.set_xlabel("$x_1$")
    ax.set_ylabel("$x_2$")
    ax.legend(loc="upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(1.01, 1), fontsize=9)  # outside
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(path, dpi=150)
    plt.close(fig)
    return int(wrong.sum())

Figure 1 with sketched boundaries — Perpendicular-bisector boundaries between neighbouring centers; circled points (20) fall on the wrong side.

3. Relation to item B. First, the threshold from item B: linear separability is lost from \(s = 1\), where the smallest separation ratio is \(r_{01} = 1.33\). At \(s = 0.5\) (\(r_{01} = 2.65\)) every pair can still be split by a line. \(r_{01}\) drops below 1 at \(s \approx 1.33\), and at \(s = 2\) (\(r_{01} = 0.66\)) three pairs are inseparable.

The region where a network necessarily makes mistakes is where the clouds overlap: points of different classes share the same coordinates, so no boundary can be right for both. As the spread grows, that region widens and fills with more points. The share of points on the wrong side of the sketched boundaries goes from 0.25% (\(s = 0.5\)) to 5.00% (\(s = 1\)), 20.25% (\(s = 2\)) and 43.00% (\(s = 4\)). The number of class pairs that no line can separate goes 0 → 2 → 3 → 5 out of 6. The sketched boundaries do not move at all, since they depend only on the means, which are fixed. What changes is how much probability mass lies beyond them, and that grows as \(r_{ij}(s) = r_{ij}(1)/s\) shrinks. A better-trained network can bend its boundaries to trade some of these errors between classes, but it cannot remove them: at \(s = 4\), 43% of the points are closer to another class's center than to their own, and five of the six pairs overlap.

Dataset I (two shifted 5-D Gaussians) is drawn with rng.multivariate_normal after checking that both covariance matrices are positive definite, and Dataset II (concentric shells) multiplies a direction \(v/\lVert v\rVert\), \(v \sim \mathcal N(0, I_5)\), by a Gaussian radius.     print(f"[2C] Dataset II: ||mean_C - mean_D|| (5-D) = {d2:.4f} (specified: 0)")

  • \(\Sigma_B\): eigenvalues \(\{0.4979, 1.0247, 1.5418, 2.1239, 2.3117\}\), minimum 0.4979.

def check_positive_definite(name, cov):
    """A valid covariance matrix must be symmetric with all eigenvalues > 0."""
    assert np.allclose(cov, cov.T), f"{name} is not symmetric"
    eig = np.linalg.eigvalsh(cov)            # eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix
    print(f"[2A] {name} eigenvalues: {np.round(eig, 4).tolist()} "
          f"-> min = {eig.min():.4f}, positive definite = {bool(eig.min() > 0)}")
    assert eig.min() > 0, f"{name} is not positive definite"
    return eig

def make_dataset_I(rng):
    """500 points of class A and 500 of class B from N(mu, Sigma) in 5-D."""
    XA = rng.multivariate_normal(MU_A, SIGMA_A, size=N_PER_CLASS)
    XB = rng.multivariate_normal(MU_B, SIGMA_B, size=N_PER_CLASS)
    X = np.vstack([XA, XB])
    y = np.repeat([0, 1], N_PER_CLASS)        # 0 = A, 1 = B
    return X, y

docs.title: B — Dataset II: concentric shells
docs.text:
For each class, 500 directions \(v \sim \mathcal N(0, I_5)\) are normalized to \(u = v/\lVert v\rVert\). The standard normal is rotation-invariant, so \(u\) is uniform on the unit sphere of \(\mathbb R^5\). Each direction is multiplied by its own radius: \(\rho \sim \mathcal N(2.0, 0.4)\) for class C (core) and \(\rho \sim \mathcal N(5.0, 0.4)\) for class D (shell), with 0.4 the standard deviation, giving \(x = \rho\,u\).

  • All 1000 directions have \(\lVert u\rVert = 1.000000\) (min and max), so the normalization is correct.
  • Measured radii: class C mean 2.010, std 0.396, range \([0.588, 2.990]\); class D mean 4.979, std 0.398, range \([3.850, 6.660]\). No radius came out negative, which would require a \(5\sigma\) draw.

# Dataset II parameters: radius rho ~ N(mean, std) for each class.
RHO_C = (2.0, 0.4)    # class C, the core
RHO_D = (5.0, 0.4)    # class D, the shell
# Threshold on ||x||^2 taken from the SPECIFIED radii, not fitted to the data:
# halfway between the two mean radii, (2 + 5) / 2 = 3.5, squared = 12.25.
RADIUS_THRESHOLD = (RHO_C[0] + RHO_D[0]) / 2
SQ_THRESHOLD = RADIUS_THRESHOLD ** 2
ex2_nonlinearity.py
def sample_shell(rng, rho_mean, rho_std, n):
    """n points x = rho * u with u uniform on the unit sphere of R^5."""
    v = rng.standard_normal((n, DIM))                    # v ~ N(0, I_5)
    u = v / np.linalg.norm(v, axis=1, keepdims=True)     # u = v / ||v||, ||u|| = 1
    rho = rng.normal(rho_mean, rho_std, size=n)          # one radius per point
    return rho[:, None] * u, u


def make_dataset_II(rng):
    """500 core points (class C) and 500 shell points (class D)."""
    XC, uC = sample_shell(rng, *RHO_C, N_PER_CLASS)
    XD, uD = sample_shell(rng, *RHO_D, N_PER_CLASS)
    # Sanity check of the construction: every direction has unit norm.
    u_norms = np.linalg.norm(np.vstack([uC, uD]), axis=1)
    print(f"[2B] ||u|| over the 1000 directions: min = {u_norms.min():.6f}, "
          f"max = {u_norms.max():.6f}")
    X = np.vstack([XC, XD])
    y = np.repeat([0, 1], N_PER_CLASS)        # 0 = C, 1 = D
    return X, y

2. Explained variance of the first two components.

Dataset PC1 PC2 PC1 + PC2 I — shifted Gaussians 50.96% 15.47% 66.44% II — concentric shells 21.66% 20.49% 42.15%

The 2-D projection of Dataset I preserves the information relevant for classification much better. In Dataset I the shift between the class means, \(\mu_B - \mu_A = [1.5]^5\), adds a large share of variance along one direction, and PCA picks it up: PC1 is almost parallel to the difference between the sample class means (\(|\cos| = 0.9923\)). The left panel of Figure 4 therefore shows A and B side by side along PC1, with an overlap band in the middle.

In Dataset II no direction is special. Both classes are rotation-invariant, so PC1 + PC2 = 42.15%, close to the 40% expected for an isotropic cloud in 5-D, and the class information, the radius, is spread over all five coordinates. Dropping three of them shrinks the radius of every point by a random amount: 61.00% of the shell points land inside the 2-D disk of radius 3.5, on top of the core (right panel). The explained variance alone does not measure class information, but here both point the same way.

3. Geometric measures in 5-D.

  • Distance between class centers, \(\lVert\hat\mu_1 - \hat\mu_2\rVert\) with sample means: Dataset I: 3.3559 (specified \(\lVert[1.5]^5\rVert = \sqrt{11.25} = 3.3541\)). Dataset II: 0.2614 (specified 0; the residual is sampling noise of the two means).
  • Figure 5, radius \(\lVert x\rVert\) of each point. In Dataset I the radii overlap: A has mean 2.130 and range \([0.456, 4.975]\), B has mean 4.223 and range \([0.951, 7.934]\). In Dataset II they are disjoint: the core's largest radius is 2.990 and the shell's smallest is 3.850, which leaves an empty gap around the dashed line \(\lVert x\rVert = 3.5\).

def center_distance(X, y):
    """||mu_1 - mu_2|| between the two SAMPLE class means, computed in 5-D."""
    return float(np.linalg.norm(X[y == 0].mean(axis=0) - X[y == 1].mean(axis=0)))


def radii(X):
    """Radius ||x|| of every point, in 5-D."""
    return np.linalg.norm(X, axis=1)


def plot_figure5(datasets, path):
    """Figure 5: radius histograms, both classes overlaid, one panel per dataset."""
    all_r = np.concatenate([radii(X) for X, *_ in datasets.values()])
    bins = np.linspace(0, all_r.max() * 1.02, 50)        # same bins in both panels
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.8), sharex=True)
    for ax, (title, (X, y, names)) in zip(axes, datasets.items()):
        r = radii(X)
        for label, name in enumerate(names):
            ax.hist(r[y == label], bins=bins, alpha=0.6, color=CLASS_STYLE[name][0],
                    edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.5, label=f"Class {name}")
        ax.set_title(title)
        ax.set_xlabel("Radius $\\|x\\|$ (5-D Euclidean norm)")
        ax.set_ylabel("Number of points")
        ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
    axes[1].axvline(RADIUS_THRESHOLD, color="black", linestyle="--", linewidth=1.5,
                    label=f"$\\|x\\|$ = {RADIUS_THRESHOLD} ($\\|x\\|^2$ = {SQ_THRESHOLD})")
    for ax in axes:
        ax.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=9)
    fig.suptitle("Figure 5 - Distribution of the radius $\\|x\\|$ per class, computed in 5-D")
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(path, dpi=150)
    plt.close(fig)

docs.title: D — Analysis
docs.text:
1. Coincident centers, separated radii: what about a hyperplane? A hyperplane classifier \(\operatorname{sign}(w^\top x + b)\) only looks at the projection \(w^\top x\). In Dataset II both classes are centered at the same point (distance 0.2614) and are rotation-invariant. Along any direction \(w\), the core (radius \(\approx 2\)) projects into about \([-2, 2]\) and the shell (radius \(\approx 5\)) into about \([-5, 5]\), both centered on 0, so the shell's projection covers the core's from both sides. Shifting or tilting the hyperplane only trades errors on one side for errors on the other. The radius histograms, in contrast, are disjoint (gap 2.990 → 3.850). The separating information is in the norm, a non-linear function of \(x\), not in any linear combination of the coordinates.

The best accuracy any hyperplane can reach is computable. One coordinate of a uniform direction on the sphere of \(\mathbb R^5\) has density \(\tfrac34(1-a^2)\) on \([-1, 1]\). Scanning the offset \(t\) of the rule "shell if \(w^\top x > t\)" for ideal radii 2 and 5 gives at best 62.01% (\(t = 1.601\)), against 50% for guessing. Applying that rule to the sample with \(w = e_1\) gives 61.50%, while \(\lVert x\rVert^2\) gets 100% (below). For contrast, on Dataset I the hyperplane that bisects the specified means \(\mu_A\) and \(\mu_B\), a linear rule with nothing fitted, already classifies 89.60% of the points.

ex2_nonlinearity.py
def f_shells(X):
    """Hand-written separator of Dataset II: f(x) = sum_i x_i^2 - 12.25.

    f(x) < 0 -> class C (core), f(x) > 0 -> class D (shell). It is linear in
    the squared inputs x_i^2 but quadratic in the original inputs x_i.
    """
    return np.sum(X ** 2, axis=1) - SQ_THRESHOLD


def best_hyperplane_accuracy_shells(r_core=RHO_C[0], r_shell=RHO_D[0]):
    """Best accuracy ANY hyperplane can reach on ideal shells (radii exactly 2 and 5).

    Both classes are rotation-invariant, so every direction w is equivalent and
    only the offset t of the rule "shell if w.x > t" matters. For u uniform on
    the unit sphere of R^5, one coordinate has density (3/4)(1 - a^2) on [-1, 1],
    hence CDF F(a) = 1/2 + (3/4)(a - a^3/3). A point of radius r lands on the
    "shell" side when u_1 > t / r, so
        accuracy(t) = [P(shell side | shell) + P(core side | core)] / 2
                    = [1 - F(t / r_shell) + F(t / r_core)] / 2.
    This is a property of the distributions, not of the sample: more data
    cannot push a hyperplane above this value.
    """
    def F(a):
        a = np.clip(a, -1.0, 1.0)
        return 0.5 + 0.75 * (a - a ** 3 / 3)
    t = np.linspace(-r_shell, r_shell, 20001)
    acc = 0.5 * ((1 - F(t / r_shell)) + F(t / r_core))
    k = int(acc.argmax())
    return float(acc[k]), float(t[k])

2. Why no linear boundary works, however much data is collected. Two finite sets are linearly separable if and only if their convex hulls do not intersect. The shell surrounds the core in every direction of \(\mathbb R^5\), so every core point is a convex combination of shell points: the core lies inside the convex hull of the shell, and no hyperplane can have all core points on one side and all shell points on the other. Collecting more data does not help. More shell points cover the sphere more densely, so the shell's hull approaches the full ball of radius \(\approx 5\) and the core sits inside it even more surely. The 62.01% ceiling above is a property of the distributions, not of the sample size; more data only estimates it more precisely. This is a limit of the model family (hyperplanes), not a lack of data.

3. PCA is linear: does a mixed 2-D projection prove inseparability? No. A projection can only lose separability, never create it. PCA is unsupervised: it keeps the directions of largest variance, not the directions that separate the classes, and it discards the rest. Points that differ only in the discarded directions collapse onto each other. My results show this directly. In Figure 4 Dataset II looks mixed: 61.00% of the shell points fall inside the core's 2-D disk, and the two components keep only 42.15% of the variance. Yet in the original 5-D space the classes are perfectly separable by a simple function of the inputs:

\[ f(x) = \lVert x\rVert^2 - 12.25 = \sum_{i=1}^{5} x_i^2 - 12.25,\qquad \hat y = \begin{cases} \text{D (shell)} & f(x) > 0 \\ \text{C (core)} & f(x) < 0 \end{cases} \]

The threshold comes from the specified radii, not from the data: halfway between 2 and 5 is 3.5, and \(3.5^2 = 12.25\). This rule classifies 1000 of 1000 points correctly (100%). It also has a wide margin: the largest \(\lVert x\rVert^2\) in the core is 8.941 and the smallest in the shell is 14.823. \(f\) is quadratic in \(x\) but linear in the features \(x_i^2\). In the lifted space \(z = (x_1^2, \dots, x_5^2)\) it is a hyperplane. That non-linear change of representation is exactly what a hidden layer can learn and a Perceptron cannot.

Preparing real-world data for a neural network. The Spaceship Titanic train.csv is loaded and described first: target balance, feature types, missing values and spending statistics, all descriptive numbers of the raw file that never feed a transformer. Then it is split 80/20, stratified by Transported, with a seed drawn from the report's rng, before any statistic is fitted. A single scikit-learn ColumnTransformer is fitted on the training split only and applied unchanged to the test split:

  • numerical columns: median imputation;
  • spending columns: TotalSpend, then \(\log(1+x)\);

  • categorical columns: most-frequent imputation, then one-hot encoding.

docs.title: A — Get to know the data
docs.text:
1. Dataset. Kaggle's Spaceship Titanic train.csv, the only labelled file: 8693 rows × 14 columns. It is read with CryoSleep and VIP as text, so all four categorical columns behave alike. This is a stateless type fix; no statistic is computed while loading.

ex3_spaceship.py
TARGET = "Transported"                       # bool: True / False
SPEND_COLS = ["RoomService", "FoodCourt", "ShoppingMall", "Spa", "VRDeck"]
NUM_COLS = ["Age"] + SPEND_COLS              # numerical features
CAT_COLS = ["HomePlanet", "CryoSleep", "Destination", "VIP"]   # categorical
DROP_COLS = ["PassengerId", "Cabin", "Name"]  # identifiers / free text: dropped
TEST_SIZE = 0.20                             # 80/20 split
ex3_spaceship.py
def load_raw(csv_path):
    """Read train.csv. Stateless type fix only: no statistic is computed here.

    CryoSleep and VIP hold True/False with gaps. Reading them as text and
    casting all four categorical columns to plain Python objects makes them
    behave the same way downstream (missing stays NaN, values become labels).
    """
    df = pd.read_csv(csv_path, dtype={"CryoSleep": str, "VIP": str})
    df[CAT_COLS] = df[CAT_COLS].astype(object)
    df[TARGET] = df[TARGET].astype(bool)
    return df

2. Goal and class balance. Each row is a passenger of the Spaceship Titanic, which collided with a spacetime anomaly. Transported (True/False) records whether that passenger was transported to another dimension. It is the target of a binary classification problem: predict it from the passenger's records.

Transported Count Share True 4378 50.36% False 4315 49.64%

The classes are essentially balanced (4378 vs. 4315 rows). Accuracy is therefore a meaningful metric, a constant guess cannot beat about 50%, and no class re-weighting is needed. Stratification still matters, because it keeps that balance identical in both splits (item B).

3. Features by type.

Type Columns Treatment Numerical Age, RoomService, FoodCourt, ShoppingMall, Spa, VRDeck median imputation, (spending: \(\log(1+x)\)), standardization Numerical (engineered) TotalSpend = sum of the five spending columns \(\log(1+x)\), standardization Categorical HomePlanet, CryoSleep (bool), Destination, VIP (bool) most-frequent imputation, one-hot Identifiers / free text PassengerId, Cabin, Name dropped, as the statement requires Target Transported (bool) label, $1 = $ True, $0 = $ False

4. Missing values per column (full train.csv, 8693 rows; descriptive only, these counts never feed a transformer):

Column Missing (count) Missing (%) CryoSleep 217 2.50 ShoppingMall 208 2.39 VIP 203 2.34 HomePlanet 201 2.31 Name 200 2.30 Cabin 199 2.29 VRDeck 188 2.16 Spa 183 2.11 FoodCourt 183 2.11 Destination 182 2.09 RoomService 181 2.08 Age 179 2.06 PassengerId 0 0.00 Transported 0 0.00

Twelve of the 14 columns have gaps, and they are remarkably uniform: between 2.06% (Age) and 2.50% (CryoSleep) each. Only the identifier PassengerId and the target are complete. No column is missing so much that it should be dropped, so every gap is imputed (item C.1).

5. Spending columns: mean, median, maximum (full train.csv, before the split). These describe the dataset as delivered and, like the counts above, are descriptive only: every statistic that a transformer uses is fitted on the training split in item C. Results-summary row 11 asks for something different, FoodCourt on the training split before transforming: mean 471.80, median 0.00 (printed after the split).

Column (full file) Mean Median Max Skewness RoomService 224.69 0.00 14327 6.33 FoodCourt 458.08 0.00 29813 7.10 ShoppingMall 173.73 0.00 23492 12.63 Spa 311.14 0.00 22408 7.64 VRDeck 304.85 0.00 24133 7.82

Mean × median reading. In all five columns the median is 0, while the means range from 173.73 to 458.08 and the maxima from 14327 to 29813. A median of 0 means at least half of the passengers spent nothing on that amenity. A mean in the hundreds therefore comes entirely from a minority, and a few passengers spent tens of times the mean or more. The distributions are extremely right-skewed and heavy-tailed, with skewness between 6.33 and 12.63 (a symmetric distribution has 0). Their spread is enormous compared with their center: the values run from 0 to tens of thousands with no typical non-zero level. Age is the contrast: mean 28.83, median 27.00, range 0–79 and skewness 0.42, only a mild right skew. On the raw spending scale a few passengers would sit far out in the tail, which motivates the \(\log(1+x)\) of item C.4.

def class_balance(y):
    """Counts and shares of each label of Transported."""
    counts = y.value_counts().sort_index()
    return pd.DataFrame({"count": counts, "share": counts / counts.sum()})


def missing_table(df):
    """Missing values per column: absolute count and percentage of rows."""
    n_missing = df.isna().sum()
    return pd.DataFrame({"missing": n_missing,
                         "percent": 100 * n_missing / len(df)}).sort_values(
                             "missing", ascending=False)


def spending_stats(X):
    """Mean, median, max and skewness of the five spending columns (NaN skipped)."""
    return pd.DataFrame({"mean": X[SPEND_COLS].mean(),
                         "median": X[SPEND_COLS].median(),
                         "max": X[SPEND_COLS].max(),
                         "skew": X[SPEND_COLS].skew()})

docs.title: B — Split before you transform
docs.text:
1. Stratified 80/20 split, fixed seed. train_test_split(test_size=0.2, stratify=y, random_state=seed). scikit-learn 1.9.1 does not accept a NumPy Generator as random_state; it raises InvalidParameterError and accepts only an int or a legacy RandomState. So the code draws an integer seed from the report's single rng right after Exercise 2, which keeps "the same rng throughout" and still gives a fixed number: seed = 579414713 on every run.

  • Result: 6954 training rows and 1739 test rows.
  • The share of Transported = True is 50.36% in train and 50.37% in test, the same as the full file (50.36%), so the stratification worked.
ex3_spaceship.py
def split(df, seed):
    """Stratified 80/20 split - the FIRST operation after loading.

    stratify=y keeps the share of Transported identical in both parts; the fixed
    seed makes the split reproducible. Nothing has been imputed, encoded or
    scaled yet, so no test-set information can leak into the transformers.
    """
    X = df.drop(columns=[TARGET])
    y = df[TARGET].astype(int)               # True -> 1, False -> 0
    return train_test_split(X, y, test_size=TEST_SIZE, stratify=y, random_state=seed)

2. Why the split comes before imputation and scaling. The test set stands in for future passengers the network has never seen, so any statistic computed with it (an imputation median, a scaling mean or standard deviation, the list of categories) would carry information about those rows into training. Splitting first and fitting every transformer on the training part only transforms the test rows exactly as new data would be. Otherwise the test score is optimistically biased (data leakage) and stops being a trustworthy estimate of generalization.

docs.title: C — Preprocess
docs.text:
The whole preprocessing is one ColumnTransformer with three per-type pipelines. preprocess() calls fit on the training split only, then transform on train and test. Every median, mode, category list, mean and standard deviation is learned from train and reused unchanged on test.

ex3_spaceship.py
def drop_identifiers(X):
    """Drop PassengerId, Cabin and Name (stateless, same on train and test)."""
    return X.drop(columns=DROP_COLS)


def add_total_spend(X):
    """Append TotalSpend = RoomService + FoodCourt + ShoppingMall + Spa + VRDeck.

    Runs AFTER imputation, so a single missing spend no longer turns the sum
    into NaN. It is a row-wise sum: there is nothing to fit.
    """
    X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
    return np.column_stack([X, X.sum(axis=1)])


def _total_spend_names(transformer, input_features):
    """Column names after add_total_spend (keeps get_feature_names_out working)."""
    return np.append(np.asarray(input_features, dtype=object), "TotalSpend")


def build_preprocessor():
    """One ColumnTransformer = three per-column-type pipelines.

    Age      : median imputation -> standardization
    Spending : median imputation -> + TotalSpend -> log1p -> standardization
    Category : most-frequent imputation -> one-hot (unknown -> all zeros)
    Columns not listed (the identifiers, if still present) are dropped.
    """
    age_pipe = Pipeline([
        ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
        ("scale", StandardScaler()),                 # (x - mean_train) / std_train
    ])
    spend_pipe = Pipeline([
        ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
        ("total", FunctionTransformer(add_total_spend,
                                      feature_names_out=_total_spend_names)),
        ("log1p", FunctionTransformer(np.log1p, feature_names_out="one-to-one")),
        ("scale", StandardScaler()),
    ])
    cat_pipe = Pipeline([
        ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")),
        ("onehot", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", sparse_output=False)),
    ])
    return ColumnTransformer(
        [("age", age_pipe, ["Age"]),
         ("spend", spend_pipe, SPEND_COLS),
         ("cat", cat_pipe, CAT_COLS)],
        remainder="drop",
        verbose_feature_names_out=False,
    )
ex3_spaceship.py
def preprocess(X_train, X_test):
    """Fit every transformer on the TRAINING split, then apply it to both."""
    X_train, X_test = drop_identifiers(X_train), drop_identifiers(X_test)
    pre = build_preprocessor()
    pre.fit(X_train)                       # medians, modes, categories, means, stds
    Xtr = pre.transform(X_train)           # learned from train only ...
    Xte = pre.transform(X_test)            # ... and re-used, unchanged, on test
    names = list(pre.get_feature_names_out())
    return pre, Xtr, Xte, names

1. Missing data, one strategy per column type (all imputers fitted on train, applied to test). Every column misses only 2.06–2.50% of its values (A.4), so a single, simple imputation per type adds little bias. A model-based imputer would add complexity for about 2% of the cells.

  • Numerical → median (SimpleImputer(strategy="median")).
    • For the five spending columns the learned training medians are all 0.0, so a missing spend becomes "spent nothing", by far the most common value: 64.0% of the observed FoodCourt values in train are 0 (Figure 6).
    • The mean would be the wrong choice here. It is dragged up by the tail (471.80 for FoodCourt on train, with skewness 6.84), so it would invent a 471.80-credit FoodCourt bill for passengers who most likely spent nothing.
    • For Age the learned median is 27.00. Age is only mildly skewed (mean 28.83 vs. median 27.00, skewness 0.42), so mean and median are close. The median is kept for robustness and consistency, and it is a real, typical age.
  • Categorical → most frequent (SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")).
    • The learned modes are HomePlanet = Earth, CryoSleep = False, Destination = TRAPPIST-1e and VIP = False.
    • The mode is the only "central value" a category has, and it keeps every one-hot block a valid indicator with exactly one active column.
    • A separate "missing" level would add four columns, one per feature, for about 2% of the rows each, so the mode is the cheaper choice at this missingness.
    • Imputation runs before encoding, so a NaN never reaches the encoder.

2. Categorical → numbers: one-hot encoding. HomePlanet, CryoSleep, Destination and VIP are one-hot encoded with OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"). The categories learned on train are Earth/Europa/Mars, False/True, 55 Cancri e/PSO J318.5-22/TRAPPIST-1e and False/True, which gives 10 one-hot columns. Each category becomes a 0/1 column, so the network sees no artificial order (Earth < Europa < Mars would be meaningless).

A category that appears only in the test set is ignored: its whole block of columns is set to 0, with no error and no new column. The row then simply carries no information for that feature, and the matrix keeps the same shape as in training. The code demonstrates it by replacing a test row's HomePlanet with the unseen value "Pluto": it encodes as HomePlanet_Earth = HomePlanet_Europa = HomePlanet_Mars = 0. In the actual split no test category is unseen; every value of the four columns in the 1739 test rows also occurs in train.

ex3_spaceship.py
def unseen_category_demo(pre, X_test):
    """Show what the encoder does with a category it never saw during fit."""
    row = drop_identifiers(X_test.iloc[[0]]).copy()
    row["HomePlanet"] = "Pluto"              # not a category of the training set
    names = list(pre.get_feature_names_out())
    block = [k for k, n in enumerate(names) if n.startswith("HomePlanet_")]
    encoded = pre.transform(row)[0, block]
    return [names[k] for k in block], encoded

3. Feature engineering: TotalSpend.

\[ \text{TotalSpend} = \text{RoomService} + \text{FoodCourt} + \text{ShoppingMall} + \text{Spa} + \text{VRDeck} \]

It is computed inside the spending pipeline after median imputation, so one missing column no longer turns the sum into NaN. It is a row-wise sum with nothing to fit, and it summarizes the overall spending level in one feature. PassengerId, Cabin and Name are dropped explicitly by drop_identifiers() before fitting. They are identifiers or near-unique strings that a network could only memorize.

4. Heavy tails: \(\log(1+x)\). The five spending columns and TotalSpend go through np.log1p. \(\log(1+x)\) maps 0 to 0, stays defined for zero spending (where \(\log x\) would be \(-\infty\)), and compresses large values multiplicatively: 100 becomes 4.6, 10 000 becomes 9.2. The before/after histogram is Figure 6 (item D.1). For FoodCourt on the training split, the skewness drops from 6.84 (raw) to 1.14 (after \(\log(1+x)\)), and the maximum shrinks from 27723 credits to 10.23.

Why it helps a network with tanh. \(\tanh(z)\) is only sensitive for \(|z|\) up to about 2–3. Beyond that it saturates at ±1 and its derivative \(1 - \tanh^2(z)\) is almost 0, so the weights feeding that unit stop learning. The code measures what standardizing the raw columns would do: the largest standardized value on the training split would be:

Column Largest standardized value, raw Largest standardized value, after \(\log(1+x)\) RoomService 22.03 2.89 FoodCourt 16.80 2.82 ShoppingMall 37.81 3.32 Spa 19.98 2.96 VRDeck 20.61 3.06

Without the log, a single passenger 37.81 standard deviations from the mean would push any unit with a non-trivial weight on ShoppingMall deep into saturation. Such values would also dominate the weighted sums and the gradients. After \(\log(1+x)\) every spending feature stays within about 3.3 standard deviations, the range where tanh still responds.

ex3_spaceship.py
def tail_compression(X_train, Xtr, names):
    """Largest standardized value of each spending column, without vs. with log1p.

    "Without": impute with the training median, then standardize the raw column.
    "With": the actual pipeline output (impute -> log1p -> standardize).
    A value of z means "z training standard deviations above the mean"; the
    larger it is, the deeper that passenger pushes a tanh unit into saturation.
    """
    out = {}
    for col in SPEND_COLS:
        raw = X_train[col].fillna(X_train[col].median())
        z_raw = ((raw - raw.mean()) / raw.std(ddof=0)).max()
        out[col] = (float(z_raw), float(Xtr[:, names.index(col)].max()))
    return out

5. Scaling: standardization (StandardScaler, \(z = (x - \text{mean}_\text{train})/\text{std}_\text{train}\)) on the 7 numerical columns: Age, the five log-spends and log-TotalSpend. The 0/1 one-hot columns are already on a tanh-compatible scale and are left as they are. Why standardization rather than min-max to \([-1, 1]\):

  • It centers every input at 0, where tanh is steepest (\(\tanh'(0) = 1\)).
  • It gives unit variance, the assumption behind the usual Xavier/Glorot initialization, so the first pre-activations start around order 1.
  • Min-max lets the extremes define the whole range: the smallest and largest training values set the scale, so a single outlier squeezes everyone else into a narrow band, and test values outside the training range break the \([-1, 1]\) promise anyway.

The resulting range is not \([-1, 1]\), but the values are of order 1, which is what tanh needs.

Split Min (scaled numerical columns) Max (scaled numerical columns) Train −2.0118 3.5156 Test −2.0118 3.5156
  • Train and test have the same extremes because both come from Age: the youngest (0 years) and oldest (79 years) passengers appear in both splits.
  • On train the scaled columns have mean 0 and standard deviation 1 by construction (the code prints them).
  • The log-spending columns stay inside \([-0.6632, 3.3172]\) on train and TotalSpend inside \([-1.1480, 1.6936]\).
  • The test set is transformed with the training statistics, so it can step slightly outside the training range: the largest test FoodCourt is 2.8479, above the training maximum of 2.8232.
  • Over the whole matrix, one-hot columns included, the range is the same \([-2.0118, 3.5156]\) in both splits.

docs.text:
1. Figure 6. FoodCourt on the training split in three stages: raw (missing values left out), after median imputation and \(\log(1+x)\), and after standardization. Each panel title prints its mean, median, skewness and share of zero spending, and main.py prints the same values. The figure also serves as the "histogram before and after" asked for in C.4.

ex3_spaceship.py
def plot_figure6(pre, X_train, Xtr, names, path):
    """Figure 6: FoodCourt on the training split - raw, after log1p, after scaling."""
    raw = X_train["FoodCourt"].dropna().to_numpy()
    # Output of the spending pipeline up to (and including) log1p, before scaling.
    spend_pipe = pre.named_transformers_["spend"]
    logged = spend_pipe[:-1].transform(drop_identifiers(X_train)[SPEND_COLS])
    logged = logged[:, SPEND_COLS.index("FoodCourt")]
    scaled = Xtr[:, names.index("FoodCourt")]

    panels = [
        (raw, "Raw FoodCourt (missing values left out)", "FoodCourt spending"),
        (logged, "After median imputation + log(1 + x)", "log(1 + FoodCourt)"),
        (scaled, "After log(1 + x) + standardization", "Standardized log(1 + FoodCourt)"),
    ]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 4.8))
    for n_panel, (ax, (values, title, xlabel)) in enumerate(zip(axes, panels)):
        ax.hist(values, bins=60, color="#2a78d6", edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.4,
                label=f"Training split (n = {len(values)})")
        if n_panel == 0:                   # raw panel: log counts make the tail visible
            ax.set_yscale("log")
            ax.set_ylabel("Number of passengers (log scale)")
        else:
            ax.set_ylabel("Number of passengers")
        s = pd.Series(values)
        mean, median, skew = (round(v, 2) + 0.0 for v in (s.mean(), s.median(), s.skew()))
        # Spending 0 is the minimum at every stage (log1p(0) = 0, then shifted).
        zeros = 100 * np.mean(values == values.min())
        ax.set_title(f"{title}\nmean = {mean:.2f}, median = {median:.2f}, "
                     f"skew = {skew:.2f}, zero spend = {zeros:.1f}%", fontsize=9)
        print(f"[3D] Figure 6 panel '{title}': n = {len(values)}, mean = {mean:.2f}, "
              f"median = {median:.2f}, max = {values.max():.2f}, skew = {skew:.2f}, "
              f"zero spend = {zeros:.1f}%")
        ax.set_xlabel(xlabel)
        ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
        ax.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=8)
    fig.suptitle("Figure 6 - FoodCourt before and after preprocessing (training split)")
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(path, dpi=150)
    plt.close(fig)

Figure 6 — FoodCourt on the training split: raw, with counts on a log scale (left); after median imputation and \(\log(1+x)\) (middle); after standardization (right).

Reading of Figure 6.

  • Raw panel (6809 non-missing values, counts on a log scale). 64.0% of the passengers spent nothing, so the first bar holds thousands of passengers. The counts then decay over several orders of magnitude, down to single passengers spending more than 20 000 credits. The mean (471.80) sits far above the median (0.00) because these few large spenders pull it up, and the x-axis must stretch to 27723 to include them. The skewness is 6.84. On a linear count axis this tail would be an almost invisible sliver.
  • Log panel. After imputation and \(\log(1+x)\) the 6954 values fit between 0 and 10.23. The non-zero spenders now spread into a broad bump instead of an invisible tail, and the skewness falls to 1.14.
  • Standardized panel. Standardization only shifts and rescales: the mean becomes 0.00, the zero spenders sit at −0.65 (the new median), and the shape and the skewness (1.14) are unchanged.
  • What no monotone transform removes. The spike of zero spenders stays a separate bar, 64.8% of the training rows once the missing values are imputed as 0 (n grows from 6809 to 6954).

2. Final checks, explicitly reported.

  • No NaN remains: 0 in the training matrix and 0 in the test matrix. The code asserts it, so the script would stop otherwise.
  • Final shape: (6954, 17) for train and (1739, 17) for test. The 17 columns are 7 numerical ones (Age, the five spending columns, TotalSpend) and 10 one-hot ones (HomePlanet 3, CryoSleep 2, Destination 3, VIP 2).
  • Value range compatible with tanh: the scaled numerical columns lie in \([-2.0118, 3.5156]\) in both splits, and the one-hot columns in \(\{0, 1\}\). Every input is centered or binary, with magnitude at most 3.52, so with small initial weights the hidden pre-activations start in the zone where tanh is responsive, far from saturation.
ex3_spaceship.py
def final_checks(Xtr, Xte, names):
    """No NaN, final shapes, and value ranges after scaling (train AND test)."""
    scaled_cols = [names.index(c) for c in ["Age", *SPEND_COLS, "TotalSpend"]]
    report = {
        "nan_train": int(np.isnan(Xtr).sum()),
        "nan_test": int(np.isnan(Xte).sum()),
        "shape_train": Xtr.shape,
        "shape_test": Xte.shape,
        # scaled numerical block (Age, 5 spends, TotalSpend)
        "num_train": (Xtr[:, scaled_cols].min(), Xtr[:, scaled_cols].max()),
        "num_test": (Xte[:, scaled_cols].min(), Xte[:, scaled_cols].max()),
        # whole matrix (the one-hot columns are 0/1)
        "all_train": (Xtr.min(), Xtr.max()),
        "all_test": (Xte.min(), Xte.max()),
    }
    assert report["nan_train"] == 0 and report["nan_test"] == 0, "NaN left after preprocessing"
    return report

3. Which decision would most affect training? The \(\log(1+x)\) on the spending columns, together with scaling them. Six of the seven numerical inputs are spending features, and without the log their largest standardized values would be 16.80 to 37.81 standard deviations from the mean, against 2.82 to 3.32 with it. Those few passengers would push tanh units into saturation, where the gradient vanishes. They would also dominate the weighted sums and the loss gradient early in training, which forces a small learning rate and slows learning for everyone else. The log turns a multiplicative scale (tens vs. thousands of credits) into an additive one that a weighted sum can use.

What the log does not fix is the zero spike: 64.8% of the training FoodCourt values remain one separate bar. The data hint at a better encoding. All 3037 passengers with CryoSleep = True have a largest recorded spend of 0.0, since cryosleepers are confined to their cabins. A binary "spent anything" flag, or a network that learns this CryoSleep–spending link, could exploit that structure. By comparison, the imputation choices touch only 2.06–2.50% of each column, and one-hot encoding four low-cardinality columns (10 columns in total) is standard and low-risk.

docs.title: 3. MLP
docs.text:
This report follows the statement's thread: what does a hidden layer buy you? Exercise 1 runs one step of backpropagation by hand. Exercise 2 trains an MLP on a binary dataset that no straight line can separate. Exercise 3 reuses the same network, unchanged, for three classes. Exercise 4 checks whether a second hidden layer helps.

  • Statement: Exercises → 3. MLP (2026.2)
  • How to re-run: from the repository root, python docs/exercises/mlp/code/main.py. It takes about a minute on a laptop CPU. It prints every number quoted below, one labelled line each, and rewrites figures/fig1.png … fig6.png. Two runs give identical output.
  • Code: code/mlp.py (the MLP, written from scratch in NumPy), code/main.py (data, baselines, training, figures) and code/check_backprop.py (a numerical check of Exercise 1). Libraries: numpy and matplotlib. scikit-learn is used only for make_blobs, make_classification, train_test_split, confusion_matrix and the LogisticRegression baselines the statement allows.
  • Seed policy: main.py creates one generator, rng = np.random.default_rng(42), and passes it through Exercises 2 → 3 → 4 in order. Every weight initialisation draws from it. The datasets use random_state=42 exactly as the statement gives them. The one exception is the multi-seed comparison of Exercise 4B, which the statement asks for. There, both architectures are initialised with the same explicit seeds, 42, 43, 44, 45 and 46. Training is full-batch gradient descent with no shuffling, so the initial weights are the only thing a seed changes.
  • Notation: the statement writes \(W^{(1)}, W^{(2)}\), and the lecture writes the same two-layer network as \(W, V\). So \(W^{(1)} \equiv W\), \(W^{(2)} \equiv V\), \(b^{(1)} \equiv b_h\) and \(b^{(2)} \equiv b_y\). Row \(i\) of \(W^{(l)}\) holds the weights of neuron \(i\), so \(z = Wx + b\).

Design decisions, shared by Exercises 2–4:

  1. One class, MLP(layer_sizes, hidden_activation="tanh", output="sigmoid" | "softmax", rng). The layer sizes are a list argument. output selects the output activation together with its matching loss: sigmoid with binary cross-entropy, or softmax with categorical cross-entropy.
  2. Full-batch gradient descent with a fixed learning rate. The training loss is recorded at every epoch.
  3. Xavier/Glorot-normal initialisation, \(w \sim \mathcal N\!\left(0,\, 2/(n_\text{in}+n_\text{out})\right)\), with zero biases. This scale keeps tanh units out of saturation at the start.
  4. Inputs are standardised with the TRAIN mean and standard deviation. The test set and the plotting grid go through the same transform, never through their own statistics.
  5. The test set is used once, for the final numbers. The hidden width and the learning rate are chosen on a validation split carved out of the training set: 75 % fit, 25 % validation, stratified, random_state=42. The rule is lowest validation cross-entropy.

docs.title: Exercise 1
docs.text:
One step of backpropagation, by hand. The network has 2 inputs, 2 tanh hidden units, 1 tanh output and the loss \(L = (y-\hat y)^2\) with \(N = 1\). Every quantity below is derived symbolically first and then evaluated. Values are rounded to 6 decimals, above the 4 the statement asks for. Each value is computed from the unrounded value before it, so redoing a step from the rounded figures can change the last digit. The script check_backprop.py repeats the arithmetic and checks every gradient against finite differences. It only verifies the hand derivation; the derivation below is the deliverable.

Given values: \(x = [0.5,\ -0.2]^\top\), \(y = 1.0\), \(W^{(1)} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.3 & -0.1 \\ 0.2 & 0.4 \end{bmatrix}\), \(b^{(1)} = [0.1,\ -0.2]^\top\), \(W^{(2)} = [0.5,\ -0.3]\), \(b^{(2)} = 0.2\), \(\eta = 0.3\), and \(\tanh'(u) = 1-\tanh^2(u)\).

docs.title: B — Backward pass
docs.text:
Each gradient applies the chain rule to the one before it. The symbolic form comes first, then the numbers.

1. Output pre-activation, \(\partial L/\partial u^{(2)}\). Start from the loss with respect to the output. From \(L = (y-\hat y)^2\):

\[ \frac{\partial L}{\partial \hat y} = -2\,(y - \hat y) = -2(0.632753) = \mathbf{-1.265507} \]

Then apply the tanh derivative: \(\hat y = \tanh(u^{(2)})\), so \(\dfrac{\partial \hat y}{\partial u^{(2)}} = 1-\hat y^{2}\), with \(\hat y^2 = 0.367247^2 = 0.134870\):

\[ \begin{aligned} \delta^{(2)} \equiv \frac{\partial L}{\partial u^{(2)}} &= \frac{\partial L}{\partial \hat y}\,(1-\hat y^2)\\ &= -1.265507 \times (1 - 0.134870) = -1.265507 \times 0.865130 = \mathbf{-1.094828} \end{aligned} \]

2. Output layer, \(\partial L/\partial W^{(2)}\) and \(\partial L/\partial b^{(2)}\). \(u^{(2)} = \sum_j W^{(2)}_j h^{(1)}_j + b^{(2)}\), so \(\partial u^{(2)}/\partial W^{(2)}_j = h^{(1)}_j\) and \(\partial u^{(2)}/\partial b^{(2)} = 1\):

\[ \frac{\partial L}{\partial W^{(2)}} = \delta^{(2)}\, h^{(1)\top} = -1.094828 \times [0.263625,\ -0.178081] = [\mathbf{-0.288624},\ \mathbf{0.194968}] \] \[ \frac{\partial L}{\partial b^{(2)}} = \delta^{(2)} = \mathbf{-1.094828} \]

3. Propagate back, \(\partial L/\partial h^{(1)}\) and \(\partial L/\partial z^{(1)}\). First the hidden activations: \(\partial u^{(2)}/\partial h^{(1)}_j = W^{(2)}_j\), so

\[ \frac{\partial L}{\partial h^{(1)}} = \delta^{(2)}\, W^{(2)\top} = -1.094828 \times [0.5,\ -0.3] = [\mathbf{-0.547414},\ \mathbf{0.328448}] \]

Then the hidden pre-activations: \(h^{(1)}_j = \tanh(z^{(1)}_j)\), so \(\partial h^{(1)}_j / \partial z^{(1)}_j = 1-(h^{(1)}_j)^2\). Here \((h^{(1)})^2 = [0.069498,\ 0.031713]\) and \(1-(h^{(1)})^2 = [0.930502,\ 0.968287]\). Element by element:

\[ \begin{aligned} \delta^{(1)} \equiv \frac{\partial L}{\partial z^{(1)}} &= \frac{\partial L}{\partial h^{(1)}} \odot \left(1-(h^{(1)})^2\right)\\ &= [-0.547414 \times 0.930502,\ \ 0.328448 \times 0.968287] = [\mathbf{-0.509370},\ \mathbf{0.318032}] \end{aligned} \]

4. Hidden layer, \(\partial L/\partial W^{(1)}\) and \(\partial L/\partial b^{(1)}\). \(z^{(1)}_i = \sum_j W^{(1)}_{ij}x_j + b^{(1)}_i\), so \(\partial z^{(1)}_i / \partial W^{(1)}_{ij} = x_j\) and \(\partial z^{(1)}_i/\partial b^{(1)}_i = 1\). This gives the outer product \(\delta^{(1)} x^\top\):

\[ \frac{\partial L}{\partial W^{(1)}} = \delta^{(1)} x^\top = \begin{bmatrix} -0.509370(0.5) & -0.509370(-0.2) \\ 0.318032(0.5) & 0.318032(-0.2) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{-0.254685} & \mathbf{0.101874} \\ \mathbf{0.159016} & \mathbf{-0.063606} \end{bmatrix} \] \[ \frac{\partial L}{\partial b^{(1)}} = \delta^{(1)} = [\mathbf{-0.509370},\ \mathbf{0.318032}] \]

Check. check_backprop.py recomputes the gradients with NumPy and compares each of the 9 scalar gradients with a central finite difference \(\big(L(\theta+\epsilon)-L(\theta-\epsilon)\big)/2\epsilon\), \(\epsilon = 10^{-6}\). The largest disagreement is \(8.3 \times 10^{-11}\).

check_backprop.py — the same chain rule in NumPy (verification only)
def forward(W1, b1, W2, b2):
    """Forward pass: z1 -> h1 -> u2 -> y_hat -> L (MSE with N = 1)."""
    z1 = W1 @ x + b1             # hidden pre-activations, shape (2,)
    h1 = np.tanh(z1)             # hidden activations
    u2 = W2 @ h1 + b2            # output pre-activation (scalar)
    y_hat = np.tanh(u2)          # network output
    L = (y - y_hat) ** 2         # squared error of the single sample
    return z1, h1, u2, y_hat, L


def backward(h1, y_hat, W2):
    """Analytic gradients, chained outward from dL/dy_hat."""
    dL_dyhat = -2.0 * (y - y_hat)            # d/dy_hat of (y - y_hat)^2
    dL_du2 = dL_dyhat * (1.0 - y_hat ** 2)   # tanh'(u2) = 1 - tanh(u2)^2
    dL_dW2 = dL_du2 * h1                     # u2 = W2 . h1 + b2
    dL_db2 = dL_du2
    dL_dh1 = dL_du2 * W2                     # each h1_j feeds u2 through W2_j
    dL_dz1 = dL_dh1 * (1.0 - h1 ** 2)        # element-wise tanh'
    dL_dW1 = np.outer(dL_dz1, x)             # z1_i = sum_j W1_ij x_j + b1_i
    dL_db1 = dL_dz1
    return dict(dL_dyhat=dL_dyhat, dL_du2=dL_du2, dL_dW2=dL_dW2, dL_db2=dL_db2,
                dL_dh1=dL_dh1, dL_dz1=dL_dz1, dL_dW1=dL_dW1, dL_db1=dL_db1)

docs.title: C — Parameter update
docs.text:
Gradient descent applies \(\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta\,\partial L/\partial\theta\) with \(\eta = 0.3\). The four update rules cover nine scalars: 2 in \(W^{(2)}\), 1 in \(b^{(2)}\), 4 in \(W^{(1)}\) and 2 in \(b^{(1)}\). All nine are listed.

Output layer:

\[ \begin{aligned} W^{(2)} &\leftarrow [0.5,\ -0.3] - 0.3\,[-0.288624,\ 0.194968]\\ &= [0.5 + 0.086587,\ -0.3 - 0.058490] = [\mathbf{0.586587},\ \mathbf{-0.358490}]\\[4pt] b^{(2)} &\leftarrow 0.2 - 0.3\,(-1.094828) = 0.2 + 0.328448 = \mathbf{0.528448} \end{aligned} \]

Hidden layer:

\[ \begin{aligned} W^{(1)} &\leftarrow \begin{bmatrix} 0.3 & -0.1 \\ 0.2 & 0.4 \end{bmatrix} - 0.3\begin{bmatrix} -0.254685 & 0.101874 \\ 0.159016 & -0.063606 \end{bmatrix}\\[4pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 0.3 + 0.076405 & -0.1 - 0.030562 \\ 0.2 - 0.047705 & 0.4 + 0.019082 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{0.376405} & \mathbf{-0.130562} \\ \mathbf{0.152295} & \mathbf{0.419082} \end{bmatrix}\\[6pt] b^{(1)} &\leftarrow [0.1,\ -0.2] - 0.3\,[-0.509370,\ 0.318032]\\ &= [0.1 + 0.152811,\ -0.2 - 0.095410] = [\mathbf{0.252811},\ \mathbf{-0.295410}] \end{aligned} \]

Does the loss go up or down? Down. A second forward pass with the updated parameters proves it:

\[ \begin{aligned} z^{(1)}_1 &= 0.376405(0.5) + (-0.130562)(-0.2) + 0.252811\\ &= 0.188203 + 0.026112 + 0.252811 = 0.467126\\ z^{(1)}_2 &= 0.152295(0.5) + 0.419082(-0.2) - 0.295410\\ &= 0.076148 - 0.083816 - 0.295410 = -0.303079\\ h^{(1)} &= \tanh(z^{(1)}) = [0.435874,\ -0.294127]\\ u^{(2)} &= 0.586587(0.435874) + (-0.358490)(-0.294127) + 0.528448\\ &= 0.255678 + 0.105442 + 0.528448 = 0.889568\\ \hat y &= \tanh(0.889568) = 0.711181, \qquad L = (1 - 0.711181)^2 = 0.288819^2 = \mathbf{0.083417} \end{aligned} \]

The loss falls from \(0.400377\) to \(0.083417\), a change of \(-0.316960\) (\(-79.17\,\%\)). The reason is that every parameter moved against its own gradient. To first order, \(L(\theta - \eta g) \approx L(\theta) - \eta\,\lVert g\rVert^2\), and \(\lVert g\rVert^2 = 1.785141 > 0\), so a small enough step must lower the loss. The first-order estimate, \(-0.3 \times 1.785141 = -0.535542\), is larger than the true drop because tanh curves the loss surface. A much larger \(\eta\) could overshoot, but \(\eta = 0.3\) does not, as the second pass shows. The individual moves all push \(\hat y\) up toward \(y = 1\):

  • \(b^{(2)}\) rose by \(0.328448\).
  • \(W^{(2)}_1\) rose where \(h^{(1)}_1 > 0\), and \(W^{(2)}_2\) fell where \(h^{(1)}_2 < 0\), so both products \(W^{(2)}_j h^{(1)}_j\) grew.
  • The hidden parameters made \(h^{(1)}_1\) larger (0.2636 → 0.4359) and \(h^{(1)}_2\) more negative (−0.1781 → −0.2941).

Together, \(u^{(2)}\) goes from 0.3852 to 0.8896.

docs.title: Exercise 2
docs.text: Binary classification a straight line cannot do. I generate the statement's three blobs and split them 80/20 with stratification. A logistic-regression baseline comes first. Then the hand-written MLP class is trained with a sigmoid output and binary cross-entropy. The hidden width and learning rate are picked on a validation split, and the test set is evaluated once. Item D explains the gap between the two models from the shape of the region in Figure 3.

docs.title: A — Generate the data
docs.text:
The generator call is the statement's, unchanged. The split is train_test_split(..., test_size=0.2, random_state=42, stratify=y). It gives 800 training and 200 test points, with 400/400 and 100/100 per class. In the test split, class 1 comes 42 points from the \((3,3)\) cluster and 58 from the \((-3,-3)\) cluster. Item D uses that imbalance.

    # A - the statement's generator, unchanged: class 0 = one cluster at the origin,
    # class 1 = two clusters at (3, 3) and (-3, -3), on opposite sides of class 0.
    centers = np.array([[0., 0.], [3., 3.], [-3., -3.]])
    X, c = make_blobs(n_samples=[500, 250, 250], centers=centers,

    X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te, c_tr, c_te = train_test_split(

main.py — standardisation and hyper-parameter selection helpers
def standardizer(X_ref):
    """Return a function that standardises with the mean/std of X_ref (the TRAIN set).

    tanh saturates for |z| >> 1, so inputs of unit scale keep the first layer in
    its responsive range. Test data is transformed with the train statistics,
    never its own.
    """
    mu, sd = X_ref.mean(axis=0), X_ref.std(axis=0)
    return lambda X: (X - mu) / sd


def targets(y, output, n_out):
    """Labels -> target matrix: column vector for sigmoid, one-hot for softmax."""
    return y[:, None].astype(float) if output == "sigmoid" else one_hot(y, n_out)


def select_hyperparameters(X_tr, y_tr, n_in, n_out, output, widths, lrs, epochs, rng):
    """Small grid search on a validation split carved out of the TRAIN set.

    The test set is never used here; it is touched once, by the final model.
    Selection rule: lowest validation loss (the cross-entropy being optimised).
    It varies smoothly, whereas accuracy on a few hundred points ties often.
    """
    X_fit, X_val, y_fit, y_val = train_test_split(
        X_tr, y_tr, test_size=0.25, random_state=42, stratify=y_tr)
    scale = standardizer(X_fit)                       # statistics of the fit part only
    rows = []
    for width in widths:
        for lr in lrs:
            model = MLP([n_in, width, n_out], output=output, rng=rng)
            model.fit(scale(X_fit), targets(y_fit, output, n_out), epochs, lr)
            val_loss = model.loss(model.forward(scale(X_val)), targets(y_val, output, n_out))
            val_acc = np.mean(model.predict(scale(X_val)) == y_val)
            rows.append((width, lr, val_acc, val_loss))
            print(f"    validation  hidden={width:>2}  lr={lr:<4}  "
                  f"val_acc={val_acc:.4f}  val_loss={val_loss:.4f}")
    best = min(rows, key=lambda r: r[3])
    print(f"    selected    hidden={best[0]}  lr={best[1]}  "
          f"({len(X_fit)} fit / {len(X_val)} validation samples)")
    return best[0], best[1]

Figure 1 — All 1000 points, coloured by class. Class 1 (orange, 500 points) is two clusters at \((3,3)\) and \((-3,-3)\) on either side of class 0 (blue, 500 points) at the origin. Crosses mark the generator's centres.
